title: 6  The quiet that wasn’t
text:
6.1 The vehicle’s two silences
Decarbonisation arrived wearing the promise of silence. The electric city would be a quiet city; the combustion engine’s roar would simply subside, and the acoustic dividend would be collected alongside the carbon one. What has happened instead is stranger and more instructive. The electric vehicle proved quiet enough at low speed to be dangerous, and is now required by law to make artificial sound. The heat pump replaces a near-silent indoor boiler with a continuous exterior hum a few metres from the neighbour’s bedroom. The wind turbine trades the power station’s remoteness for a rhythmic swish over rural dwellings. This is the distributed transition — felt at the doorstep, one installation at a time — and it is the necessary counterpart to the concentrated transition of Chapter 7, where the same energy system pools its sound into single, vast, humming sites.
The paradox deserves precise formulation, because it is easily flattened into either of two false versions. The false pessimistic version says the transition is making things louder; taken as a whole, it is not, and nothing in this chapter should be read as a case against decarbonisation. The false optimistic version says electrification is an acoustic policy; it is not that either, and the sections that follow show why. The accurate version is narrower and more interesting: the energy transition redistributes sound across space, time and frequency. It withdraws a source that was loud, intermittent and concentrated along roads, and introduces sources that are quieter, continuous and scattered across kerbsides, gardens and horizons. Whether any particular window ends up better or worse off depends on where it sits in that redistribution.
Three properties recur across the three sources examined here, and they are worth naming in advance because they are what the redistribution consists of. Each new source is quieter than the one it displaces, which is the reason the promise of silence was plausible. Each is more continuous, which means the relief of the interval — the gap between one lorry and the next — is what the transition actually removes. And each sits closer to the dwelling, or is tonal, or is modulated, which is to say that each has more of its character in the parts of the signal an annual A-weighted average is least equipped to record. The metrics were tuned to the source that is leaving. That mismatch was set out in Chapter 2 in its cleanest form and reaches its fullest expression in Chapter 7; here it is not an argument to be made but a condition to be worked in.
The electric car has two silences, and only one of them was ever real. Below roughly 20 km/h it is markedly quieter than its combustion predecessor — quietly enough that the difference became a pedestrian-safety problem, and the law moved to fill the gap. Above that speed the silence is largely a fiction, because what a light vehicle mainly emits at urban cruising speed is not its engine but the contact between its tyres and the road, and that source is indifferent to what turns the wheels. The first silence had to be legislated away; the second needs no legislation, because it never existed. Between them they define both the size of the acoustic dividend electrification actually pays and the narrow band of conditions under which it is paid at all.
Take the first silence. For a century, vehicle sound regulation ran in one direction only: downward, capping the maximum a machine might emit. UNECE Regulation No 138, adopted in 2016, runs the other way. It requires pure electric and hybrid vehicles capable of moving without their combustion engine to carry an Acoustic Vehicle Alerting System — a loudspeaker, in effect — generating sound automatically from start-up to approximately 20 km/h and when reversing, precisely because the vehicles’ reduced audibility endangers pedestrians, cyclists and above all visually impaired road users (United Nations Economic Commission for Europe, 2017). The regulation prescribes minimum overall levels that rise with speed — 50 dB(A) at 10 km/h, 56 dB(A) at 20 km/h, 47 dB(A) in reverse — so that a listener can judge not merely presence but behaviour, together with a mandatory frequency shift as the vehicle accelerates and a ceiling of 75 dB(A) to keep the cure from reproducing the disease (United Nations Economic Commission for Europe, 2017). In the European Union the requirement entered through Regulation (EU) No 540/2014, whose Annex VIII was rewritten to incorporate the UNECE provisions: mandatory for new vehicle types from July 2019 and for all new electric and hybrid vehicles from July 2021 (European Commission, 2017; European Parliament and Council of the European Union, 2014).
The EU text adds a stipulation of genuine acoustic-cultural interest. The generated sound should be continuous, should indicate the vehicle’s behaviour, and should be “similar to the sound of a vehicle” of the same category fitted with an internal combustion engine (European Commission, 2017). The machine designed to retire the engine is required to impersonate it. This is not nostalgia written into law but an admission about perception: a century of exposure has trained urban ears to parse one particular spectrum as approaching car, and the trained response is a safety asset too valuable to discard along with the technology that produced it. The engine is being decommissioned as a power source and retained as a signal.
Two readings of AVAS should be held apart. Read as safety engineering, it is uncontroversial and evidently sensible. Read as measurement politics, it is a quiet landmark: the first occasion on which the regulatory apparatus, having spent decades defining noise as an excess to be capped, found itself legislating a minimum — conceding, in legal text, that sound carries information whose absence is itself a hazard. Floor and ceiling now sit in the same annex, and the distance between them, 56 to 75 dB(A) at 20 km/h, is the entire band within which the electric vehicle is permitted to exist acoustically. The unwanted sound of one framework is the safety-critical signal of the other, and the same decibels are being counted twice with opposite signs.
The second silence dissolves under measurement, and the reason was met at the close of Chapter 5: above modest urban speeds the tyre, not the engine, is what a light vehicle is heard by. The campaign of Pallas and colleagues, undertaken to extend the CNOSSOS-EU emission model to electric vehicles, put numbers to what that dominance implies for electrification: at 30 km/h the electric car was on average 2.6 dB quieter than its combustion counterpart, and above 40 km/h the difference had collapsed to between 0.4 and 1.6 dB — within touching distance of nothing, and well inside the tolerance the Directive itself allows on emission inputs (Pallas et al., 2016). A companion study of tyres representative of electric-vehicle fitment found rolling noise to be the main source even at 20 km/h (Czuka et al., 2016). Seen against these figures, the R138 threshold is not an arbitrary administrative round number but a codified acoustic judgement: 20 km/h is the speed above which the regulator assumes the tyre will announce the vehicle unaided (United Nations Economic Commission for Europe, 2017). The two silences meet exactly at the point where the law stops speaking.
The diagnostic consequence is easily stated and widely underestimated. Electrifying the fleet does not quieten the street wherever traffic moves faster than roughly 30 km/h. What it changes is the spectrum — the low-frequency bands where the engine lived subside, while the mid-frequency broadband of rolling noise remains — and, with it, the composition of the residual problem, which becomes a matter of pavements, speed and tyre design rather than powertrains. It is also, incidentally, an argument already won by the 30 km/h urban limit: the only regime in which the electric fleet’s acoustic dividend is actually paid out is one in which vehicles spend most of their time at speeds where propulsion still matters. The quiet electric city is available, but it has to be driven slowly into being.

title: 6  The quiet that wasn’t
section: 6.2 The heat pump on the party wall
text:
6.2 The heat pump on the party wall
If the electric vehicle rearranges the street, the air-source heat pump rearranges the garden fence. Acoustically it is a fan and a compressor running for long stretches of the day and, unlike the gas boiler it replaces, mounted outdoors — often within a few metres of a neighbour’s bedroom window, and frequently against a wall or in the corner formed by two, each reflecting surface adding to the level at the receiver. What it emits is not loud by any traffic standard. It is continuous, it carries tonal components, its energy sits low in the spectrum, and it is placed exactly where the domestic soundscape used to be at its quietest, at exactly the hours when the surrounding street is at its own quietest.
Each of those four properties works against the instrument used to assess it. A continuous source has no events to count and no gaps to lose; averaged over a day it can be reported as modest while never once affording relief. A tonal component is what the ear locks onto and the broadband total dilutes. Low-frequency energy is precisely what A-weighting is built to discount, by some 16 dB at 125 Hz and 26 dB at 63 Hz, as recalculated in Chapter 2. And a source that matters most when everything else falls silent is a source whose significance is a matter of contrast rather than level — which no absolute threshold, however carefully negotiated, is constructed to see. This is in miniature the profile that returns at industrial scale in Chapter 7: quiet by the numbers, intolerable in the room.
The complaint statistics have begun to register it. In its 2026 data briefing, covering October 2024 to September 2025, the Chartered Institute of Environmental Health recorded noise complaints about air-source heat pumps as a distinct source for the first time: 103 complaints across England and Wales, concentrated in the South West, against a total of just under 307,000 noise complaints of all kinds (Chartered Institute of Environmental Health, 2026). One hundred and three is a small number, and should be reported as one — a rounding error in the national ledger, three complaints in ten thousand. Its significance is not magnitude but appearance. Categories in complaint statistics behave rather like species in a census: the year in which one is first recorded separately matters independently of its initial abundance, because it marks the moment at which an administrative apparatus decided the thing was distinct enough, and likely enough to grow, to deserve a line of its own. The count is small because the installed base is small; the installed base is the variable that policy is actively trying to enlarge.






NoteForty-two becomes thirty-seven



The governance response has been unusually quick, and its form is instructive. In Britain, a domestic heat pump may be installed without planning permission provided a standardised sound calculation — distance, reflecting surfaces, barriers — shows the level at the nearest neighbour’s window to fall below a fixed threshold. In March 2025 the standard governing that calculation, MCS 020, was split in two and revised, and the threshold tightened from 42 to 37 dB(A) (The MCS Service Company, 2025). Five decibels is a substantial correction: a cut of roughly two-thirds in the sound energy a compliant installation may deliver to the neighbour. It was conceded not because heat pumps had grown louder but because the earlier limit, set when installations were few, proved too permissive once they multiplied.
The revision is a small, complete specimen of something that recurs throughout these chapters. A threshold looks like a scientific constant and behaves like a negotiated settlement — one that holds while the population of sources is sparse and is reopened when that population grows. Note also what the tightening does not address: tonality, and the character of the sound rather than its level. The number moved; the quantity being counted did not. The interactive later in this chapter implements the underlying arithmetic and lets both thresholds be tested against any unit, distance and siting.

title: 6  The quiet that wasn’t
text:
6.3 The turning blade
The third new source stands furthest from the window and generates the longest arguments. Wind-turbine sound is aerodynamic in origin, dominated by the interaction of the blade with the air, and its most distinctive feature is amplitude modulation: a periodic rise and fall of the level at the blade-passing rhythm, the swish that distinguishes a turbine from any steady industrial source (C. Hansen & Hansen, 2020). Modulation matters because hearing is built to notice change rather than constancy. A fluctuating sound is more salient than a steady one of identical average level — and average level is exactly the quantity the assessment records. The modulation depth can be several decibels while the mean moves not at all.
The field evidence points where the mechanism predicts. A year-long study at dwellings near two Australian wind farms found that residents’ annoyance reports clustered overwhelmingly at night and in the early morning, and that in at least half of the recorded episodes the sound was described as swish or swoosh (K. L. Hansen et al., 2021). Two features of that result deserve attention. The complaints track a descriptor — a quality of the sound — rather than a level; and they concentrate in the hours when atmospheric conditions favour modulation and background sound is lowest, which is to say in the period the assessment framework covers least well.
The guidance registers this source with unusual, and revealing, hesitancy. The WHO’s 2018 environmental noise guidelines — the same document whose road-traffic recommendations anchor Chapter 3 — issue for wind turbines only a conditional recommendation, that average exposure be kept below 45 dB \(L_\text{den}\), the conditionality reflecting the limited body of high-quality evidence (World Health Organization Regional Office for Europe, 2018). For night-time exposure no recommendation is offered at all: the evidence was graded too low to support one. And the guidelines volunteer a caveat that repays slow reading. Describing this source through \(L_\text{den}\) or \(L_\text{night}\), they concede, “may be a poor characterisation of wind turbine noise” and may limit the very ability to observe associations between it and health outcomes (World Health Organization Regional Office for Europe, 2018).
The concession is made in the instrument’s own founding document, by the instrument’s custodians, and its logic runs in a circle worth tracing slowly. The indicator averages away the modulation; the modulation is what the evidence suggests does the annoying; studies built on the indicator therefore struggle to find the association; the association, unfound, is graded as weak evidence; the weak grading yields a merely conditional recommendation — and the indicator is retained, because it is the indicator, and because a conditional recommendation is not the sort of finding that displaces a measurement standard. The 58 Hz tone of Chapter 2 vanished into the A-weighted total by the same arithmetic. No further comment is offered here; the governance chapter of Part III will collect the interest on this deposit.
What the indicator averages away can still be made audible. The synthesiser below generates a wind-turbine-like sound and lets its amplitude modulation be raised or lowered; crucially, it holds the mean level fixed, so the modulated and steady versions share an identical \(L_\text{eq}\) — the very quantity the assessment records. One of them is far harder to ignore than the other.

The source is no abstraction in Andalusia. At the close of 2025 the region counted 158 wind farms totalling some 3,712 MW of installed capacity, and the zones approved under Spain’s maritime spatial plans for future offshore wind lie principally off the coasts of Málaga, Granada and Almería (Agencia Andaluza de la Energía, 2026). The turbines of the energy transition are not someone else’s horizon.

title: 6  The quiet that wasn’t
text:
6.4 Composing the net-zero street
The argument can now be handed to the reader, because it is an argument about combination and combination is what arithmetic does better than prose. The simulator below assembles a decarbonised street from the components verified in the preceding sections and sets it against its own combustion baseline. The traffic module implements the CNOSSOS-EU category-1 emission model with the coefficients as amended in 2021, treating electric vehicles as rolling noise plus the R138 minimum below 20 km/h (European Commission, 2021; Pallas et al., 2016; United Nations Economic Commission for Europe, 2017). The heat-pump module implements the distance-and-reflection arithmetic of the MCS calculation and tests the result against both the former 42 dB and the current 37 dB thresholds (The MCS Service Company, 2025). The turbine module propagates a declared sound power across open ground against the WHO’s conditional 45 dB guideline (World Health Organization Regional Office for Europe, 2018). Three modules of input; one window as output.
Three behaviours are worth provoking deliberately. Set the traffic to 50 km/h and slide the electric share from nothing to everything: the façade level barely moves, and the spectrum below shows precisely why — the electric bars fall away at 63 and 125 Hz and hold their ground at 1 and 2 kHz. Drop the speed to 20 km/h and the dividend appears at last, some four and a half decibels of it. Then quieten the street altogether and watch the heat pump and the turbine — sources that would once have drowned unnoticed in traffic — surface as the loudest things at the window.

AVAS minima: UNECE Regulation No 138 (United Nations Economic Commission for Europe, 2017). Electric-vehicle treatment follows Pallas et al. (2016). That last behaviour is the chapter’s thesis in operational form, and it is worth stating without the interface. The new sources do not become audible because they grow. They become audible because the thing that masked them is withdrawn — which means the transition manufactures its own complainants, and does so most reliably where it succeeds best. A street that electrifies its traffic and warms its houses with compressors has not exchanged a loud soundscape for a quiet one. It has exchanged an intermittent, familiar, broadband, publicly owned sound for a continuous, novel, tonal, privately owned one, and has moved the source from the road to the boundary wall — from a thing the council is responsible for to a thing the neighbour is.

title: 6  The quiet that wasn’t
text:
6.5 Designing the transition’s sound
The soundscape of the net-zero street is not an accident that befalls the energy transition. It is a design outcome, and at the time of writing it is still being decided — in type-approval annexes, in permitted-development thresholds, in setback distances, in the March revision of a calculation standard most people will never read. The window in which such defaults are set is brief, and it is open now.
What makes this worth saying, rather than merely lamenting, is that every source examined here is more governable than the one it replaces, not less. The AVAS spectrum is specified by regulation, which means it could in principle be specified well: nothing but convention requires a synthetic warning to imitate a combustion engine rather than to be designed, from first principles, as a signal that is maximally detectable and minimally annoying. The heat pump’s siting is a published formula with distance, reflection and screening as its terms — three levers, all available at the survey stage and all cheaper before installation than after. The turbine’s modulation is an active field of research with engineering levers attached (C. Hansen & Hansen, 2020). The combustion engine offered none of this: its sound was a by-product of thermodynamics, and could be muffled but not composed. The sources of the transition are, for the first time, authored — which is the practical reason the design turn of the final chapter belongs in Part III as the natural completion of the diagnosis, and not merely as aspiration.
One boundary must be drawn honestly before moving on. Everything examined here is small, near and numerous: a loudspeaker per bumper, a compressor per garden, a turbine per ridge. Each is quiet on its own terms; the burden is the sum, and the sum accumulates one planning decision at a time. The same transition has another face — singular, vast and continuous — in which the electricity for the vehicles and the models alike is consumed in windowless halls that hum at frequencies the A-weighted map barely registers. The distributed transition has been audited. The concentrated one is next.

title: 7  The machine hum
text:
7.1 The 24/7 drone
The distributed transition has been audited; the concentrated one is next. Where the distributed transition of Chapter 6 reached a million separate doorsteps — an alerting system bolted to a silent car, a heat pump breathing on a party wall — the digital transition arrives as a single large object that never switches off. A data centre does not roar. It hums: a steady tone compounded from cooling fans, chillers, transformers and the periodic exercising of standby generators, as present at three in the morning as at three in the afternoon, on every day of the year. People who live beside these buildings tend to describe a sound they feel as much as hear — a pressure in the room, a rumble that seems to rise through the floor rather than arrive through the window — and to report that it is worst at night, once the traffic that masked it by day has thinned away. The operator’s instrument, set to the standard weighting and averaged across the day, frequently returns a figure comfortably inside the local limit. That gap, between an intrusion residents insist is severe and a number the regulation calls acceptable, recurs in every case that follows. It is not the signature of a single badly sited plant. It follows from what the standard metric was built to record and, more consequentially, from the part of the spectrum it was built to leave out — the same low band in which, in Chapter 2, a 58 Hz tone could be watched slipping out of the A-weighted reading while remaining plainly present in the spectrum.
The acoustic problem begins with a difference in kind, not only degree. Road traffic, the dominant burden of Chapter 5, is intermittent and broadband: it rises and falls with the passing vehicle and spreads its energy across the audible range. The plant that cools a large data hall does neither. It runs continuously, and a substantial share of its output is concentrated into a few narrow frequency bands — the blade-passing tones of banks of fans, the harmonics of transformers, the drone of chillers — which the ear resolves as a definite pitch rather than a wash. Steady, tonal and low: these three properties, taken together, describe a sound that human listeners find disproportionately hard to ignore, and one that the built environment does little to hold back, since low frequencies pass through the walls and windows that would stop a higher-pitched noise (Leventhall, 2004). Constancy compounds the effect. A sound that never pauses offers the ear no respite and no contrast, and it removes the intervals of quiet against which a household organises rest; the absence of variation, which the averaged metric treats as benign, is exactly what residents report as intolerable.
At the property line, the numbers look modest. A 2024 review of Virginia’s data-centre corridor, where roughly four-fifths of the state’s capacity is concentrated in three northern counties, placed the sound reaching nearby homes in a band of about 40 to 59 dB(A) — a range that reads, on paper, like a quiet suburban street (Joint Legislative Audit and Review Commission, 2024). The same review likened what reaches those homes to the low, continuous hum of air-conditioning plant — a phrase that registers both the character of the sound and its constancy, and that already marks it off from the intermittent noise the surrounding zoning had been framed to address (Joint Legislative Audit and Review Commission, 2024). The lived account is harsher. In Prince William County, where a decades-old ordinance caps residential noise at 60 dB(A) by day and 55 by night but exempts heating and cooling equipment, residents beside a cluster of data centres recorded their own measurements well above those limits — averages around 62 dB(A) and night-time peaks near 69 — while the facilities remained, on the operator’s reading, within the rules (Prince William Times, 2024). The discrepancy is not mysterious once the character of the sound is admitted: a steady 62 dB(A) tone at three in the morning is a different creature from a 62 dB(A) figure produced by daytime traffic, and an ordinance written to catch parties and modified exhausts cannot tell the two apart (Joint Legislative Audit and Review Commission, 2024).
The extreme cases make the mechanism legible. In Chandler, Arizona, close to a decade of complaints against the air-conditioning tone of a large campus produced first noise-reducing retrofits, then, in 2022, a zoning amendment requiring sound studies before any new facility, and finally, in 2025, a council vote to refuse a proposed data centre outright — a municipal reversal driven substantially by noise (Environmental and Energy Study Institute, 2025). Cryptocurrency mining, which packs tens of thousands of processors and their cooling fans into open-sided halls, supplies the loudest instances. Beside a 300-megawatt bitcoin operation in Granbury, Texas, residents recorded readings that ran into three figures — one household measured 103 dB(A) — against a state threshold that treats 85 dB(A) as the point of unreasonableness and caps the penalty at a five-hundred-dollar fine; the sound has been likened to a jet engine that never lifts off, and it carries for miles, waking sleepers who live well outside any plausible buffer zone (Chow, 2024). In the Bono community near Greenbrier, Arkansas, the fans of some seventeen thousand machines a few hundred feet from the nearest house pushed readings to 82 dB(A), around the clock, in a state that had just passed a law forbidding local governments from regulating such operations at all — a preemption its legislature partially reversed a year later, once the complaints had become impossible to set aside (Lenora, 2024). The bitcoin cases sit at the extreme, but they are the same object magnified: banks of fans cooling banks of processors, and no off switch.
These are American cases because the American build-out came first and largest, but the concentrated transition has now reached Andalusia. In June 2026 the first stone was laid, in the Escúzar technology park south of Granada, of SP01: a campus built expressly for artificial-intelligence training and high-performance computing, with around 100 MW of gross grid capacity granted and roughly 70 MW of it destined for the servers themselves, ramping from a first phase of some 10 MW, through an intermediate stage of around 25 MW, toward full build-out by the end of the decade (DataCenterDynamics, 2026). Its acoustic signature is, for now, a matter of design rather than complaint, and two of its stated design choices bear directly on that signature: the campus is to draw on renewable power and to cool its densest racks with direct liquid cooling rather than air. Liquid cooling matters here for a specific and non-rhetorical reason — moving heat in a closed loop of fluid displaces a large part of the fan bank whose blade-passing tones are the usual source of the drone. The point is not that the Granada campus will be silent, nor that its arrival is unwelcome; it is that the tonal, low-frequency character of the hum is set at the drawing board, in decisions about cooling and siting taken before the first server is powered, and is therefore still open in a way that the metric applied afterwards is not.

title: 7  The machine hum
text:
7.2 The infrasound controversy
Below the audible drone lies a more contested claim: that these installations also emit infrasound — pressure fluctuations below about 20 Hz, at or beneath the threshold of conscious hearing — and that this inaudible component is itself a cause of ill health. The claim recurs wherever large rotating or pumping machinery sits near homes, and the evidence around it has a characteristic shape, one already met in Chapter 6’s account of wind farms. It divides, roughly, into three postures.
The first minimises. A body of work, some of it produced with support from the industries whose installations are under scrutiny, concludes that measured infrasound levels near such sites fall below the threshold of perception and can therefore be dismissed as a source of symptoms (Berger et al., 2015). The reasoning is not empty — perception thresholds at very low frequencies are real and steep — but the provenance warrants the same caution one would bring to any assessment funded by an interested party, and the conclusion tends to treat below the average threshold of perception as equivalent to without effect, which is a stronger claim than the data support.
The second finds an effect and hedges it. Controlled exposure of volunteers to low-frequency and infrasonic tones has been reported to shift markers of autonomic function — heart-rate variability, the balance of sympathetic and parasympathetic activity — in directions consistent with a mild stress response (Chiu et al., 2021). Such studies are suggestive, but they are typically small, brief and conducted under laboratory conditions that do not reproduce the years-long, sleep-interrupting exposure residents describe; a measurable change in a physiological marker over an hour is not the same as a demonstrated pathway to disease over a decade.
The third is neutral and technical, and it is the most useful of the three. A detailed measurement study of large wind turbines established that as rotating machines grow, the balance of their emitted spectrum shifts downward: the relative share of low-frequency energy rises, and even after A-weighting a substantial part of what remains sits at the bottom of the range, with the loudest third-octave band for several machines falling at or below 250 Hz (Møller & Pedersen, 2011). The finding concerned turbines, not data halls, but the physics is general and the parallel is exact: the larger and more powerful the source, the more its acoustic weight migrates into precisely the band that ordinary assessment handles worst.
The defensible position, on the present evidence, is that the complaints are real and the specific attribution to infrasound is not settled. People living beside these facilities are not imagining the sound; the readings confirm a persistent, tonal, low-frequency presence, and the reported symptoms — broken sleep, headache, difficulty concentrating — are well-attested consequences of chronic low-frequency noise whether or not any inaudible sub-20 Hz component contributes (Leventhall, 2004). What remains genuinely open is whether infrasound as such, rather than the audible low-frequency noise that accompanies it, does independent physiological harm. Holding those two questions apart is not pedantry. It is the difference between a claim the evidence can carry and a claim it cannot — and, as the argument from the instruments below makes clear, the weaker of the two is not the one on which the case against the metric depends.

title: 7  The machine hum
section: 7.3 Why the metre cannot hear it
text:
7.3 Why the metre cannot hear it
The reason the operator’s number and the resident’s experience diverge is built into the number itself, and it can be stated without recourse to any disputed physiology. Two operations are applied to almost every regulatory measurement of environmental noise, and each, independently, discards the part of the signal in which the data-centre hum lives.
The first is A-weighting. The standard sound-level reading, dB(A), is not a neutral record of acoustic energy; it is energy passed through a filter that mimics the reduced sensitivity of the human ear at low frequencies, and that filter rolls off steeply below a few hundred hertz (International Electrotechnical Commission, 2013). A pure tone at 50 or 60 Hz — the region where transformer hum and the lower blade-passing tones sit — is cut by the weighting curve by tens of decibels before it is ever compared with a limit. Chapter 2 made this visible directly, following a 58 Hz tone as it dropped out of the A-weighted figure while remaining plainly present in the spectrum. The second operation is temporal averaging. The indicators that anchor most noise law, Lden and its night-time counterpart, integrate sound energy across long periods, so that a source which is perfectly steady — the defining property of a data centre — is smoothed into a single background value rather than flagged as the relentless, unvarying presence that makes it unbearable. Weighted to discount the frequencies and averaged to discount the constancy, the metre is, in a precise sense, deaf to the two features that define the complaint.
This is the point at which care matters most. The case here is not that infrasound has been proven to sicken people; that claim, as the previous section granted, is unsettled. The case is narrower and far more secure: the instrument used to certify these facilities as compliant is systematically blind to the band of the spectrum that generates the complaints. The first proposition is a contested question in physiology. The second is a demonstrable property of a filter and an averaging window, and it holds regardless of how the physiology is eventually resolved. A steady 58 Hz tone can be, at once, the dominant feature of a resident’s night and nearly absent from the dB(A) reading that governs whether anything can be done about it. That even A-weighted spectra from large low-frequency sources keep their peak energy at the bottom of the range (Møller & Pedersen, 2011) is not a curiosity; it is confirmation that the weighting does not merely soften the low end but can misplace where the sound’s energy actually lies.
The corrective tools exist, which is itself telling. Assessment procedures written specifically for low-frequency complaints — the kind developed for national environmental agencies precisely because the ordinary metric was failing — measure in narrow low-frequency bands and test them against dedicated criteria rather than a single A-weighted figure (Moorhouse et al., 2005). And where a clearly audible tone is present, some schemes add a penalty of up to six decibels to the assessed level, on the reasoning that a pure tone annoys more than its bare energy would predict — the same logical correction applied, in Chapter 6, to the tonal and amplitude-modulated character of wind-turbine noise. The Spanish noise regulation sets exactly that six-decibel ceiling for an emergent tone, and identifies the tone on the unweighted third-octave spectrum rather than on the A-weighted figure that governs compliance (BOE, 2007).
The existence of these corrections is an admission, encoded in the standards themselves, that the default metric under-reads tonal low-frequency noise. Yet it is the default metric, not the corrective procedure, that is written into most compliance regimes; the operator is judged by the instrument that cannot hear the sound, and the burden of demonstrating the sound falls on the residents, who must produce their own measurements to capture what the official method was built to pass over. In Prince William, the officials revising the county’s code said as much in plain terms: the low-frequency noise the data centres emit is not fully captured in A-weighted decibels (Prince William Times, 2024). When a measurement regime reliably yields compliant numbers for a sound that reliably yields complaints, the question of whom that arrangement serves answers itself.

title: 7  The machine hum
text:
7.4 Distance and the tonal hum
Why the hum reaches homes that look, on a map, comfortably far from the plant is a question of how sound of different pitches survives the journey. Two mechanisms strip energy from a source as distance grows. The first, geometric divergence, is indifferent to frequency: the same spreading loss applies to a low tone and a high one alike as the wavefront expands. The second, atmospheric absorption, is strongly frequency-dependent — the air itself converts sound to heat, and it does so far more efficiently at high frequencies than at low. A crisp, high-pitched noise loses its edge within a few hundred metres; a deep tone loses almost nothing to the air and is checked only by spreading. Distance therefore acts as a filter, stripping away the treble and leaving the bass, so that the further one stands from a broadband industrial source the more purely tonal and low its remaining sound becomes. This is why a data-centre or mining hum can be reported from a mile or more away as a rumble rather than a roar, and why it is often the households that moved out precisely for quiet who are worst affected.
The interactive model below makes the trade-off explicit. Setting a source level, a frequency and a distance, the reader can compare how a low tone and a high one decay, and can watch the A-weighted figure fall away from the actual sound-pressure level as the frequency is lowered — the same divergence between what is present and what is counted, now expressed in metres of separation rather than in a single reading at the fence.

title: 7  The machine hum
text:
7.5 The energy of the hum
The hum is, in the end, the sound of electricity being turned into computation and heat. Fans spin because processors run hot; processors run hot because the calculation is vast and unremitting; and cooling, the single largest non-computing draw in most facilities, is the immediate source of the noise. The acoustic signature is thus a fairly direct readout of the energy appetite that the author’s work on the power demand of artificial-intelligence infrastructure has traced elsewhere (Moreno-Muñoz, 2026): a campus sized in tens or hundreds of megawatts is, by that very sizing, committed to moving a proportionate quantity of waste heat, and the ordinary way to move it is to push air across metal at scale. The design choice on display at Escúzar — liquid rather than air — is significant precisely because it breaks that chain at the fan; but it does not lighten the underlying load, since the heat still leaves the building and the energy still enters it. As AI-scale campuses grow denser, the quantity of heat to be shifted grows with them, and with it the pressure on whatever mechanism moves it.
This makes the concentrated transition a double object, an energy story and an acoustic one told in the same breath, and it sets up the two chapters that follow. The sound does not stop at the property line. It passes through the walls that would stop a higher-pitched noise and settles into bedrooms and living rooms — the terrain of the indoor and personal soundscape, where the same low-frequency physics meets sleep, attention and the private spaces least equipped to exclude it. And the recurring pattern of these cases — a real intrusion, a compliant number, an ordinance built for a different kind of noise, and, in Arkansas, a law that briefly forbade the affected communities from regulating the source at all before a partial retreat — is a preview of the governance problem in its sharpest form. The regulatory architecture assembled to contain environmental noise leans on exactly the metric this source is built, whether by accident or by convenience, to slip past. Why that architecture fails the new sources, and what the mismatch between an old instrument and a changed acoustic world reveals about how noise is governed, is the matter to which Part III returns. The machine hum is the clearest case in these pages of a sound loud enough to drive people from their homes and quiet enough, by the measure that counts, to be officially inaudible.

title: 8  The indoor and the personal
text:
8.1 Intelligibility, not loudness
The machine hum of the previous chapter did not stop at the wall; it settled into rooms. Indoors, environmental noise changes what it costs. On the street it is counted in premature deaths and broken sleep; in the rooms where people learn and work it is counted in something quieter and far harder to see — a sentence half-heard, a paragraph read twice, a train of thought broken and not recovered. Here noise is rarely loud. It is the ventilation drone of an open-plan office, the hard echo of an under-treated classroom, the traffic bleeding through a single-glazed window, the private wash of a pair of headphones. What it degrades is intelligibility and attention rather than comfort, and the children still learning to read carry that cost least evenly. The temptation is to let noise stand in for distraction in general; the discipline here is to keep it acoustic — a measurable signal competing with a measurable background — and to follow what that competition does to understanding.
The quantity that matters indoors is not how loud the background is in absolute terms, but the margin between the speech a listener is trying to follow and the background it must be separated from — the speech-to-noise ratio — together with the time the room takes to fall quiet after a sound, its reverberation time. Both are ordinary acoustic measurements; neither is a metaphor. A library at forty decibels and a canteen at forty decibels are identical on a sound-level reading and worlds apart in what can be understood in them, because understanding depends on the relation between voice and background, not on the background alone.
The two quantities degrade comprehension by different routes. A high background masks the quieter parts of speech directly, burying the consonants that carry most of its meaning while the louder vowels, which carry less, survive. A long reverberation time does something subtler: it smears each sound forward in time, so that the tail of one syllable overlaps the onset of the next and the boundaries between words dissolve. A room can therefore be perfectly quiet and still hard to follow, if it rings; the two faults are independent, and a space has to control both. Acousticians fold them into a single figure, the Speech Transmission Index, which runs from zero to one and rises as the combination of a favourable speech-to-noise ratio and a short reverberation time preserves the modulations of speech on their way from mouth to ear. The index is banded for interpretation: a value above roughly 0.75 counts as excellent and one below about 0.45 as poor, with the range between them marking the distance between a room a listener follows without effort and one in which every sentence has to be partly reconstructed (International Electrotechnical Commission, 2020).
The recommended values for a classroom are unambiguous. The international standard sets a background at or below 35 dB(A) in the unoccupied room, a reverberation time at or below 0.6 seconds, and a speech-to-noise ratio of at least fifteen decibels at the pupil’s ear — a combination that corresponds to a Speech Transmission Index of about 0.6, the floor below which intelligibility is judged inadequate for learning (Acoustical Society of America, 2010). It is worth setting that figure beside the domestic legal objective. Spain’s noise regulation fixes the interior target for a classroom at 40 dB, five decibels above the level the acoustic evidence recommends (BOE, 2007). The gap is small in decibels and large in consequence, and it is a first sign of a pattern this account has met before — the number written into law sitting a comfortable margin away from the number the evidence would set. The same index recurs in every room that follows. What changes, from the classroom to the office, is not the physics but the goal.

title: 8  The indoor and the personal
text:
8.2 The classroom
A child does not listen the way an adult does. An adult who misses a word rebuilds it from the surrounding sentence, from grammar, from expectation; a seven-year-old still assembling those resources has less to fall back on, and so needs a cleaner signal to reach the same understanding. This is why the margin recommended for a classroom — a speech-to-noise ratio of at least fifteen decibels — is wider than an adult would require (Acoustical Society of America, 2010). Some children need it wider still. A child learning in a second language, or with a hearing loss, a developmental disorder, or the fluctuating middle-ear congestion common in early childhood, has even less spare capacity to reconstruct a degraded signal; the acoustic conditions that merely inconvenience a confident native speaker can shut such a child out of the lesson altogether. A standard written for the average pupil is, for them, already a compromise (Acoustical Society of America, 2010). The cost of failing to provide it is not a single misheard instruction but a chronic tax on the effort of listening, paid out over the years in which reading and attention are being built.
The mechanism is one of effort. Following speech in noise is not automatic; it draws on working memory and sustained attention to hold the fragments of a sentence while the missing pieces are inferred. A favourable acoustic environment makes that reconstruction cheap, and a poor one makes it expensive, levying a continuous charge on the same cognitive resources a lesson is meant to build. For an adult the charge is usually affordable. For a child it competes directly with the work of learning to read, and because the exposure is chronic — the same classroom, the same road outside, day after school day — the small daily costs accumulate into a measurable lag. Nor does the pathway run through attention alone: the autonomic and stress responses described in Chapter 3 operate here too, so that a noisy classroom taxes a child bodily as well as cognitively, throughout the years in which the capacities under strain are still forming.
The evidence that the tax is real, and not merely plausible, has accumulated steadily. The systematic review prepared for the World Health Organization’s environmental noise guidelines examined thirty-four studies of noise and cognition, every one of them conducted on children, and found evidence of moderate quality that chronic exposure to transport noise is associated with poorer reading comprehension and impaired memory (Clark & Paunović, 2018). The scale of the burden, once those relations are applied across the continent, is not small: European environmental agency estimates attribute to transport noise more than half a million cases of reading-comprehension impairment among European children, alongside tens of thousands of cases of behavioural difficulty (European Environment Agency, 2025).
Two studies anchor the association in Spain, and they complement each other. The older, foundational one is the RANCH project, which measured aircraft and road-traffic noise at schools around three European airports — Heathrow, Schiphol and Madrid-Barajas — and related exposure to children’s reading comprehension, establishing an exposure-effect relation in which comprehension declined steadily as noise rose, consistently across the three countries (Clark et al., 2006). The more recent is a Barcelona cohort that followed 2,680 primary-school children, aged seven to ten, across thirty-eight schools over a year, tracking the development of their working memory and attention against the road-traffic noise measured at their schools. Children at the noisier schools progressed more slowly on every cognitive test; the association held for noise at school but not for noise measured at the children’s homes, which points to the classroom, where the sustained work of learning is done, as the place where the exposure bites (Foraster et al., 2022). One detail of that study reaches past the classroom and toward the argument built through these chapters. It was not the average noise level that tracked most closely with slower progress, but the fluctuation of the noise — the peaks. The children exposed to the sharpest swings, not merely the highest means, fell furthest behind, a distinction the close of the chapter returns to (Foraster et al., 2022).
The cost is not distributed evenly, and its unevenness is not accidental. Land beside a motorway, a rail corridor or a flight path is cheaper, and the schools and housing built on it more often serve families with the least room to choose otherwise, so that the acoustic burden falls, with grim regularity, on the children for whom an additional handicap is hardest to carry. The pattern is not universal — a case that runs the other way appears in Chapter 9 — but for the transport noise that fills a child’s school day, exposure and disadvantage tend to move together.
Granada has no study of its own. What it has is an exposure map. The city’s strategic mapping puts fewer than about 26,000 residents — under eleven per cent of a resident population of roughly 234,000 — above 65 dB in the day–evening–night average (El Independiente de Granada, 2023; INE, 2025). That ceiling, though, is set against the permissive national quality objective rather than the lower levels the World Health Organization treats as health-relevant: measured against those, road traffic alone leaves close to a third of the city above 50 dB at night, and more than half above 55 dB by day — in other words, around 78,000 residents are affected at night under the WHO‑relevant threshold (El Independiente de Granada, 2023).
Its schools sit within that same acoustic geography, and for those on the most exposed streets the exposure-effect relations found in Barcelona and around Madrid would, on the same mechanism, predict a comparable cost to working memory and attention among their pupils — an expectation, not a measurement, and one no one has yet tested locally.

title: 8  The indoor and the personal
text:
8.3 The office and the headphone
The adult indoor world turns the classroom problem on its head. In a school the aim is to make one voice, the teacher’s, as intelligible as possible to everyone in the room. In an open-plan office the aim is the reverse: to make the many voices at neighbouring desks as unintelligible as possible to everyone not party to them. The same physical quantity governs both, but the target is inverted, and the reason lies in a well-documented quirk of attention. It is not loud speech that most degrades cognitive work, but intelligible speech. A conversation one can make out — whether or not one wants to — recruits the language faculties involuntarily and competes for the very resources a written task requires; the same conversation reduced to an unintelligible murmur largely stops interfering. The disturbance tracks intelligibility, not volume.
The room-acoustic standard for open-plan offices is built directly on this finding. It defines a distraction distance: the distance from a speaker at which the Speech Transmission Index of their voice falls below 0.50, the point beyond which their speech is no longer intelligible enough to seriously disrupt a neighbour (International Organization for Standardization, 2022). The same standard describes how quickly speech should fade across a floor — the rate at which its level falls with each doubling of distance from the talker — and treats a high rate of decay, won through absorptive ceilings, screens and soft floors, as the mark of a well-designed open plan. The aim is counter-intuitive: not to make the office quiet, which would leave every telephone call legible from thirty desks away, but to raise the background just enough, and let speech decay fast enough, that the words at any distant desk arrive already blurred.
How much is at stake is itself quantified. A model widely used to set the criterion relates the decrement in cognitive performance to the intelligibility of the intruding speech, and finds the relation steepest across the mid-range of the index — performance falls away rapidly as intelligibility climbs from about 0.25 to about 0.60, then flattens. The penalty is bounded but not trivial: at the worst intelligibilities the modelled loss on a demanding task settles at around seven per cent, a tax paid quietly and continuously by everyone on the floor (Hongisto, 2005). It follows that the two indoor problems demand opposite remedies from the same firm. The money spent on a training room or a workplace crèche goes to raise the index, pulling a single voice clear of the background; the money spent on the open floor next door goes to lower it, pushing every voice down into indistinctness. Absorption, screening and deliberately added masking sound all serve the second end — not silence, which would leave every whisper legible, but a background just dense enough to render the words at the next desk indistinct.
The headphone is the individual’s answer to both problems, and it carries its own. Worn at a desk, it is a refuge — a private soundscape that masks the office and restores some of the control the open plan took away. Worn on the street or the train, it is an exposure. The volumes people choose to overcome ambient noise are frequently high enough to matter: the World Health Organization estimates that around 1.1 billion young people are at risk of hearing loss from unsafe listening, roughly half of them through personal audio devices (WHO, 2019). The boundary of safe listening is set at 80 decibels for adults, and lower — 75 — for children, over a working week’s exposure (World Health Organization & International Telecommunication Union, 2019). The dynamic is self-reinforcing, for the louder the surroundings, the higher the volume a listener sets to ride above them, so that the noisiest environments — the very ones headphones are used to escape — draw the largest self-administered doses. And the safe dose falls steeply as the volume climbs — about forty hours a week at 80 decibels, roughly four hours at 90, some twenty minutes at 100 — so that a level chosen to override a loud train buys minutes, not hours, before it begins to wear on hearing. It is why the safe-listening standard now adopted for personal devices builds in dose tracking and volume limits rather than trusting a listener’s own sense of what is loud (World Health Organization & International Telecommunication Union, 2019). A systematic review pooling data from across twenty countries put the global number of adolescents and young adults potentially at risk, from personal devices and loud venues together, at somewhere between 0.67 and 1.35 billion (Dillard et al., 2022). The instrument most people reach for to take command of their own soundscape is thus also, for a great many of them, a self-administered dose — the private end of a public problem, and the point at which the exposure becomes something a person does to themselves rather than something done to them.

section: 8.5 The cost that does not show up on a metre
text:
8.5 The cost that does not show up on a metre
A strategic noise map records the level at a façade. It does not record whether the child behind that façade finished the paragraph, or whether the clerk two floors up read the clause twice, or how much of the effort a room demanded was spent simply on hearing rather than on thinking. The indoor cost of noise is real, it is measurable in principle, and it is almost entirely absent from the monitoring that governs environmental noise, which stops at the outer wall and reports an annual average of what it finds there. The quantity that does the damage indoors — the moment-to-moment margin between a voice and its background — is precisely the quantity that outdoor mapping is not built to see.
The Barcelona finding sharpens the point. The children who fell furthest behind were not simply those exposed to the highest average level but those exposed to the sharpest fluctuation, the peaks (Foraster et al., 2022). An indicator built by averaging sound energy over a day, a year, a lifetime, smooths those peaks into a single background figure and reports the room as quieter than the experience of being in it — the same operation, applied to a different room, that let a steady tone disappear from a compliance reading two chapters ago. Whether the source is a data centre or a passing lorry, the averaging that makes a metric governable also makes it partly blind to the feature that carries the cost.
That cost does not stay acoustic for long. A reading age not reached, an attention span not built, a working memory that develops a year behind where it might have — these convert, over a lifetime, into measurable disadvantage in earnings, in health, in the opportunities a person can take. And they fall, more often than not, on the same people twice over: the household beside the busy road absorbs the outdoor burden of disturbed sleep and raised cardiovascular risk, and sends its children to the school where the indoor burden is heaviest, the two exposures compounding rather than cancelling. What that compounded cost is worth, who ends up paying it, and whether the arithmetic could justify the price of quieter schools and quieter offices, are questions of value rather than acoustics. They belong to the economics of quiet and to the unequal distribution of exposure — the matter to which Part III now turns.

title: 9  Sonic injustice
text:
9.1 The expected pattern
There is a tempting story about noise and justice, and it is half true. The tempting story says noise falls, like other environmental harms, most heavily on the poor — that the map of exposure is the map of deprivation. In many places it is: studies in the Netherlands and the United States find heavier burdens in deprived and minority neighbourhoods. But noise does not always behave like air pollution, and the honest version of the justice argument is more interesting than the slogan. In Barcelona between 2007 and 2014, and under the aircraft corridors over London, exposure ran higher among the more affluent — the inverse of the pollution pattern. That inversion is not an awkward exception to be explained away but the finding itself: the geography of noise is real, unequal, and irreducible to a single axis.
The slogan earns its force honestly, because in a great many settings the burden really does track disadvantage. The most comprehensive single body of evidence comes from the United States, where a nationwide model of noise exposure found levels consistently higher in neighbourhoods with lower income and lower educational attainment, and higher again where the Black, Hispanic and Asian populations were larger; racial segregation compounded the effect, so that the loudest places were the poor, segregated ones (Casey et al., 2017). The pattern recurs in Europe. A national study of the Netherlands, spanning more than nine thousand neighbourhoods, found environmental noise higher where incomes were lower, employment scarcer and the residents more often of non-Western migrant background — the same social gradient, on the other side of the Atlantic (Hayward & Helbich, 2024). Reviews of the wider literature record the same tendency, at least where deprivation is measured directly (Trudeau et al., 2023).
The mechanism is largely a matter of where the loud things were put. Major roads, rail corridors, flight paths and industrial sites tend to run through or beside the cheaper land — which is to say the land occupied by those with the least power to refuse them — an arrangement produced over decades by the ordinary workings of land value and planning, and in some places by outright discrimination in how neighbourhoods were zoned, served and mortgaged. The infrastructure that carries a city’s noise was routed, again and again, away from the districts that could resist it and toward those that could not. What looks on a map like an accident of geography is often the residue of who held power when the road was drawn. The same asymmetry runs through the decisions taken since. Which streets are pedestrianised, where a barrier is raised, whose complaint is logged and acted upon — these are settled in planning processes to which the poorest residents have the least access and the faintest voice, so that the distribution of noise is shaped not only by where the powerless were placed but by how little say they have had in moving it since (Trudeau et al., 2023).
Exposure, moreover, is only half of the disadvantage. Once the noise arrives, the capacity to keep it out is itself unequally distributed, and along the same lines. Older and cheaper housing comes with thinner walls and single glazing; the double-glazed window, the flat that faces the courtyard rather than the avenue, the move to a quieter street, the second home to retreat to — each is a way of buying quiet, and each is rationed by income. Tenure sharpens the divide, since a renter cannot readily retrofit a building that is not theirs, and time deepens it, since those with the fewest options to be elsewhere spend the most hours inside the exposure. The disadvantaged household therefore tends to receive more noise at the façade and to stop less of it at the wall — a compounded penalty that a map of outdoor exposure does not even register. Where this is the shape of things, the slogan is simply true, and the injustice is of the familiar kind.

title: 9  Sonic injustice
text:
9.2 The inversion
It is not always the shape of things. In Barcelona, environmental noise over the years 2007 to 2014 was distributed in the opposite direction from air pollution measured in the same city: the pollutants were heaviest in the more deprived neighbourhoods, as the intuition predicts, but noise exposure was higher in the more affluent ones (Saez & López-Casasnovas, 2019). A dedicated mapping of the city’s noise inequity located the loudest conditions in the central districts — the dense, mixed, sought-after core rather than the poorer periphery (Lagonigro et al., 2018). And the pattern is not peculiar to Spain. In London, the odds of living inside the fifty-decibel contour of aircraft noise were highest for residents with the highest household income, the lowest area-level deprivation, and white ethnicity — a clean reversal of the environmental-justice expectation. Tellingly, the same study found rail noise running the other way, more common among Black residents than white: two sources, two opposite social gradients, within a single city (Tonne et al., 2018). Reviews of the evidence describe the cross-city picture as frankly mixed, the social gradient of noise pointing in opposite directions in different places (Trudeau et al., 2023) — which is itself the point.
The reason noise can behave this way is that it attaches to the very things that make a location desirable. Density, centrality, street life, the constant traffic of a place where people want to be — these generate sound, and they are also what commands a premium. Central districts carry, on top of their traffic, a further layer the periphery is largely spared: the noise of leisure and nightlife, the terraces and venues that cluster where the crowds are. The lively inner district is loud precisely because it is lively; the calm lies at the edges, in the peripheral estates and the low-density, leafy uptown. To live where the action is, in most cities, is to pay for it partly in decibels, and those who can afford the centre are buying the noise along with the amenity. That premium is capitalised into rents and prices, which complicates the language of choice. The owner who buys into a loud central district has in some sense chosen its noise; the tenant priced into the same building, or the long-standing resident who cannot afford to leave as the district grows expensive around them, has chosen nothing. Even in the affluent centre, the exposure and the power to escape it need not be held by the same hands.






NoteThe terrace, up close




The ordinance and its judicial lifeNeighbourhood associations and the ombudsman routeThe overtourism link


The terrace is not an unregulated gap; it is regulated and repeatedly re-litigated. Madrid’s 2022 ordinance, which relaxed the terms on which hospitality terraces could occupy public space, was annulled by the Madrid High Court for having skipped the environmental and budgetary assessments the law requires [ECLI:ES:TSJM:2024:3559], a ruling the Supreme Court left standing on appeal; a new ordinance took effect only in late 2025, with the interval governed by the older, less permissive 2013 rules (Ayuntamiento de Madrid, 2025; Tribunal Superior de Justicia de Madrid, Sala de lo Contencioso-Administrativo, Sección Segunda, 2024). Palma’s own ordinance names the tension in its own preamble, presenting itself as an attempt to reconcile the city’s economic development and tourist nature with residents’ right to rest (Ajuntament de Palma, 2014). And the friction is not confined to tourist capitals: a neighbourhood federation took Palencia’s terrace ordinance to the Castile and León courts on the same grounds — excessive occupation of public space at residents’ expense — a reminder that the underlying conflict is about public space and rest, tourism only sharpening it where it is already most contested (Tribunal Superior de Justicia de Castilla y León, Sala de lo Contencioso-Administrativo, 2026).


Where litigation is slow or costly, residents’ associations have increasingly gone to the ombudsman instead. In Zaragoza, the Stop Ruido Casco Histórico association took its complaint to the regional Justicia de Aragón in 2025, naming both hospitality terraces and the short-term tourist lets multiplying around them, clustered against heritage-listed buildings in the historic centre (European Network of Ombudsmen, 2025). In Alicante, a residents’ association’s complaint led the regional ombudsman to find the city’s 1991 noise ordinance inadequate to the leisure-district noise it now faced, and to recommend the city consider declaring an acoustically saturated zone under the Directive’s own domestic tool (Síndic de Greuges de la Comunitat Valenciana, 2023). And in 2023 Spain’s national ombudsman opened the same file simultaneously against Madrid and Barcelona, asking each for a programme of scheduled, unannounced inspections rather than one that waits on a resident’s complaint (European Network of Ombudsmen, 2023).


The pattern these disputes trace out has a name in the recent literature: overtourism does not arrive as noise alone, but noise is consistently among the costs it imposes on the people who live where it lands. A peer-reviewed study of Málaga found long-term residents identifying noise pollution alongside rent inflation and diminished access to public services as the burden of a tourism model whose gains accrue chiefly elsewhere, and linked that burden to a wider erosion — of affordable housing, of neighbourhood continuity, of the historic fabric itself — that residents experienced as a slow expulsion from their own city (Siyamiyan Gorji et al., 2026). The terrace, in that light, is not a nuisance incidental to a successful tourist economy; it is one of the more audible ways that economy’s costs are distributed onto those least positioned to charge for them — the same distributive logic this chapter traces at the level of the whole city, heard here at the scale of a single street.





Barcelona’s own current figures make the shape of it concrete. Taking the ten districts, and the share of each district’s residents exposed to a day-evening-night level at or above sixty-five decibels, the loudest by a wide margin is l’Eixample — the dense, central, relatively affluent grid — where roughly thirty-eight per cent of residents live above that level. The quietest include Nou Barris, one of the city’s humblest districts, at under fourteen per cent; the wealthy but peripheral Sarrià-Sant Gervasi sits well below l’Eixample despite having by far the highest incomes. Across the ten districts the correlation between household income and noise exposure is positive, and it does not soften as the threshold rises: restrict attention to the very loudest exposure, above seventy or seventy-five decibels, and the concentration in the wealthier districts grows stronger, not weaker (Ajuntament de Barcelona, 2022; Ajuntament de Barcelona, Oficina Municipal de Dades, 2019).
None of which means that wealth produces noise, or that the gradient is clean. The driver is centrality and density; income enters only because the central, dense districts happen to be the desirable and expensive ones. The relationship frays at the edges accordingly. Ciutat Vella, the old town, is central and far from wealthy yet relatively quiet, its tight and partly pedestrianised streets carrying less traffic than the great avenues to the north; the wealthiest district is not the loudest, and one of the poorest is not the quietest. The inversion is a tendency, not a law — which is exactly why it resists the single-axis story, in either direction. There is a temporal dimension that a single snapshot hides. As heavy industry has left the inner city and the centre has gentrified, the geography of noise and the geography of deprivation, once more nearly aligned, have in places pulled apart: the factory that once punished a working-class district is gone, while the traffic and nightlife that replaced it now fall on a district that has since grown wealthier. The inversion is, in part, a record of what cities have become.

title: 9  Sonic injustice
section: 9.3 Why noise is not air pollution
text:
9.3 Why noise is not air pollution
Noise and air pollution share their principal source — the motor vehicle — and yet they come to rest in different places, and the difference is instructive. A pollutant, once emitted, disperses: it drifts on the wind, accumulates in still air, settles over whole districts, and concentrates where the dirty infrastructure was sited, which is disproportionately where the poor live. Noise neither drifts nor accumulates. It radiates from its source and falls away steeply with distance, halving and halving again over a few hundred metres, so that it attaches not to a region downwind but to a place — to the specific, dense, trafficked fabric that produces it. Pollution is a fog that pools in the low ground of the social landscape; noise is a property of the ground itself, and the desirable ground is often the loud ground.
This is why an environmental-justice framework built on the model of pollution does not transfer cleanly to sound. The pollution model assumes that a hazard flows toward the powerless, and prescribes moving the burden back up the gradient. Noise can flow toward the powerful — not because it seeks them out, but because they have chosen to live amid the density that makes it. A politics of noise that simply imports the pollution script, hunting for the burdened poor and redistributing the harm upward, will in a city like Barcelona be aiming in the wrong direction, and will miss the people it most needs to reach.
For the deeper complication is that being more exposed and being more harmed are not the same thing. The same Barcelona analysis that found noise heavier in the affluent neighbourhoods also found the risk of dying from environmental hazards markedly lower there — on the order of thirty per cent lower in the most affluent areas — because the residents of the poorer neighbourhoods were more susceptible to a given exposure, carrying worse baseline health, more overlapping exposures and less capacity to recover from any of them (Saez & López-Casasnovas, 2019). The susceptibility is not mysterious. A body that meets a night of broken sleep already worn by insecure work, poorer diet, untreated illness and the chronic stress of scarcity has less reserve to absorb the added load — and it rarely meets the noise alone, for the loud street is often also the polluted one, the overcrowded flat, the neighbourhood with the fewest green places to recover in. The harms stack, and they stack on the same people. Exposure and impact can therefore diverge: the affluent may take in more noise and suffer less from it, while the deprived take in less and suffer more. A justice defined purely on exposure would then reach a perverse destination — that the first duty is to shield the already-advantaged from their self-chosen decibels — while the people bearing the heavier bodily cost went unattended.
There is a further dimension the exposure map cannot see at all. Sonic injustice, on the fullest account, is not only the unequal distribution of unwanted sound but the unequal distribution of access to wanted sound — to quiet, to restorative and pleasant acoustic environments, to the plain ability to govern what one hears (Trudeau et al., 2023). On that axis the advantage runs the ordinary way, and runs sharply. The affluent household, even where the street outside is loud, can buy its way inward to quiet through glazing and a courtyard-facing room, and outward to the good soundscapes — the garden, the calm park, the house in the hills — that the poor cannot reach. Its exposure is, in a sense, chosen and escapable; the exposure of the poor is neither. Measured only at the façade, the injustice looks scrambled; measured by who can command quiet when they need it, it resolves back toward the familiar direction. Both are true at once, and neither alone is the whole of it. It is also the half of the problem least examined. The evidence on who bears unwanted sound is by now substantial; the evidence on who is denied access to wanted sound barely exists — a single study set against dozens (Trudeau et al., 2023). What is not measured tends not to be governed, and the access gap has so far been largely neither.

title: 9  Sonic injustice
text:
9.5 Justice without a single axis
If the burden of noise runs one way in one city and the other way in the next, and if being more exposed is not the same as being more harmed, and if the power to obtain quiet is distributed differently again, then it is no longer obvious what a just distribution of quiet would even be. It cannot be simply the redistribution of noise away from the poor, because in some cities the poor are already the quieter. It cannot be equal exposure for all, because equal exposure would ignore both the unequal susceptibility that makes the same decibel more damaging to some, and the unequal access to quiet that persists whatever the façade reading says. Each simplification, pressed against the evidence, gives way.
What is left, once they fall away, is a more demanding and more honest object. A just soundscape would protect the most susceptible before the most exposed, since it is the susceptible who convert a given noise into the greater loss of health. It would treat access to quiet — a restful bedroom, a nearby calm park, the plain ability to escape sound when one needs to — as a good that ought not to be rationed by income. And it would refuse to load the heaviest exposure onto those least able either to keep it out or to recover from it, even where, on the raw map, they are not the most exposed of all. That is a distributional standard with several axes rather than one, and no single map will satisfy it. In practice it would pull policy in more than one direction at once — toward glazing and barriers for the exposed poor, toward new quiet places in the districts that have none, toward protecting the susceptible neighbourhood even when its façade readings are not the city’s highest — and it would judge success not by the average decibel brought down but by whether those least able to secure quiet for themselves had at last been helped to it.
It also sets the terms for what follows. Whether protecting quiet is worth its cost — whether the health, the productivity and the plain liveability recovered by a quieter city justify the price of achieving it — is a question of value, and belongs to the economics of quiet. Why the instruments meant to govern noise, tuned as they are to a single averaged number at the façade, so reliably miss both the susceptibility and the access that no exposure figure records, is a question of governance. The distribution is only the first of the three.
